families.s: HSE risk-based supervision of young children in swimming pools
families.t: under-eight children, adult supervision, pool size, depth gradient, access, staffing, swimming ability and session type
f: Health and safety law does not prescribe one universal adult-to-child ratio for young swimmers.
Operators should decide safe admission arrangements through risk assessment.
The assessment should consider children under eight during unprogrammed sessions.
Pool-tank size is relevant to supervision decisions.
The gradient and range of water depth should be considered.
Access routes and the wider pool environment affect supervision.
Staffing levels should be considered.
Children's swimming capability should be considered where possible.
families.g: Young-child pool risk depends on age and swimming ability, adult supervision, group size, pool geometry and depth, access, session type, crowding, staffing and emergency capability.

families.s: HSE swimming-pool disinfection and chemical-exposure management
families.t: microorganisms, disinfectants, by-products, water treatment, dosing, storage, plant rooms, exposure control, competence and emergency response
f: Swimming-pool disinfection is necessary to control harmful microorganisms.
Properly managed pools should keep chemical and by-product exposure low for bathers and workers.
Water-treatment arrangements should follow recognised technical standards.
Chemical selection and dosing should reflect pool use and system design.
Incompatible treatment chemicals should be kept apart and controlled during storage and handling.
Plant-room ventilation and access controls should reflect credible release hazards.
Workers handling treatment chemicals need suitable information, training and protective measures.
Emergency procedures should cover leaks, dosing failures, contamination and unsafe water conditions.
families.g: Pool-chemical risk depends on chemical and concentration, dosing and storage, ventilation and plant layout, water demand, maintenance, exposure route, competence and emergency arrangements.

families.s: HSE prevention of suction entrapment at swimming-pool sump outlets
families.t: single outlets, suction, second sumps, interlocks, alternative lines, grilles, inspection, maintenance and shutdown
f: A single pool sump outlet can create suction-entrapment risk if covered by a swimmer's body.
Operators should modify pools where assessment identifies this risk.
A second outlet can reduce the chance that one person covers the entire suction path.
Outlets should be separated sufficiently so one swimmer cannot cover both.
A pressure-operated interlock can stop the pump after a significant suction-pressure change.
A permanently open alternative suction line from a spillway or drain can reduce entrapment risk.
Grille covers should be securely fixed across sump outlets.
Outlet covers, interlocks and pumps require inspection, maintenance and prompt defect response.
families.g: Sump-entrapment risk depends on outlet number and spacing, pump suction and flow, grille design and condition, interlocks and alternative lines, swimmer body size, inspection and maintenance.

families.s: HSE respiratory-hazard controls in laundries and dry cleaners
families.t: chlorine, hypochlorite, ammonia, sulphur dioxide, filter powder, contaminated laundry, fumes, dust, ventilation and RPE
f: Laundry and dry-cleaning workers can inhale hazardous fumes, dusts and fibres.
Examples include chlorine and hypochlorite fumes.
Ammonia and sulphur-dioxide exposure can irritate the respiratory system.
Filter powders and other airborne solids can create inhalation hazards.
Laundry may arrive contaminated with hazardous material such as asbestos.
Occupational asthma and respiratory irritation are recognised sector risks.
Exposure should be reduced through process control and effective ventilation.
Suitable respiratory protection should be provided where residual powder or fume exposure cannot be adequately controlled otherwise.
families.g: Laundry respiratory risk depends on chemicals and contamination, process and temperature, release form, ventilation and LEV, task duration, cleaning, RPE, maintenance and worker susceptibility.

families.s: HSE COSHH essentials for dry cleaning with chlorinated solvent and spot cleaning
families.t: enclosed machines, solvent loading, unloading, leaks, spot cleaning, ventilation, storage, PPE, spills, maintenance and training
f: HSE provides COSHH essentials sheets for dry cleaning with chlorinated solvent.
Separate guidance covers solvent-based spot cleaning.
All listed control points should be followed or replaced by equally effective measures.
Tetrachloroethene can be absorbed by inhalation and through the skin.
Very high exposure can occur while dry-cleaning machines are loaded or unloaded.
Breath biological monitoring can help verify whether exposure remains controlled.
Results approaching or exceeding guidance values should trigger more frequent monitoring and investigation of control effectiveness.
Dry-cleaning machines should be maintained, checked for leaks and supported by spill procedures and worker training.
families.g: Dry-cleaning solvent risk depends on solvent and concentration, machine enclosure and leaks, loading and unloading, spot-cleaning method, ventilation, skin contact, monitoring, maintenance and competence.
